claims.text: Annealing-induced changes in Q235 grain-boundary structure control the formation, continuity, and adherence of protective oxide scales.
Grain-boundary structure affects oxide-scale behavior by altering oxygen-diffusion pathways.
Varying annealing duration at approximately 800 °C in air will produce Q235 samples spanning a range of grain sizes and grain-boundary densities.
Grain-boundary density and distribution modulate oxygen-diffusion paths in Q235.
Higher grain-boundary density in refined Q235 microstructures accelerates oxygen diffusion.
Accelerated oxygen diffusion in refined Q235 promotes formation of a continuous oxide layer at high temperature.
The oxide layer promoted by a refined Q235 microstructure will be more adherent and uniform.
Coarser-grained Q235 will form more discontinuous oxide scales.
Discontinuous oxide scales on coarser-grained Q235 may spall or permit continued corrosion.
Optimized refined-grain Q235 will develop smoother and more uniform oxide scales than untreated or coarser-grained Q235 during hot-salt exposure.
Optimized refined-grain Q235 will exhibit lower mass change than untreated or coarser-grained Q235 during hot-salt exposure.
Optimized refined-grain Q235 will have greater high-temperature corrosion resistance than untreated or coarser-grained Q235.
The proposed grain-boundary-mediated protection is less pronounced at room temperature because oxidation kinetics are slower.
The proposed mechanism is expected to be dominant during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
At room temperature, grain-boundary density is expected to have minimal influence on oxide formation because diffusion is slower.
Other microstructural factors and impurities in Q235 may alter the quantitative relationship between grain-boundary density and corrosion performance.
